subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Mathematics as Pattern-Finding: The Ten Sequences

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.2
textbook_items_in_class.description: Think of other examples where mathematics helps in everyday life (shopping, cooking, speed, area, design, etc.).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Recognise the formation pattern in each of the ten number sequences listed in Table 1.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Rewrite each sequence from Table 1 with the next three terms, and write the rule for each sequence in own words.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.2
homework.description: Explain how mathematics has propelled humanity forward, citing examples across scientific experiments, economy, infrastructure, technology, and timekeeping.

time_bands.activity: Open with the framing from section 1.1: mathematics is, in large part, the search for patterns and the explanations behind them. Invite students to brainstorm using Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.2 ("Think of other examples where mathematics helps in everyday life…."), collecting ideas on the board — shopping totals, cooking ratios, tiling patterns, clock faces — to ground the idea that pattern-finding is both creative and practical.

Direct students to Table 1 in section 1.2. Working in pairs, they tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.3 ("Recognise the formation pattern in each of the ten number sequences….") — students study each row in silence, then whisper their rule to their partner before a brief class share. Pay particular attention to Virahānka numbers, naming Virahānka as the Indian mathematician for whom the sequence is named.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.3 ("Rewrite each sequence from Table 1 with the next three terms, and write the rule…."). After writing, pairs compare their rules for triangular numbers, squares, and cubes, discussing why the rules differ in form. Circulate and prompt: 'How do you know your rule works for the fourth term and not just the first three?'

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the triangular number rule (adding successive counting numbers) with the square number rule (adding successive odd numbers); listen for this during pair-sharing and address it by asking students to compute the difference between consecutive terms of each sequence. Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.2 ("Explain how mathematics has propelled humanity forward….") is set as take-home written reflection to allow fuller articulation than class time permits. The self-study pointer for confident students is the Virahānka sequence: they may try writing a rule connecting each term to the two before it.

periods.activity_title: Dot Diagrams: Seeing Why Names Fit

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Copy each pictorial representation from Table 2 and draw the next picture in each dot-diagram sequence.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain geometrically why 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … are called triangular numbers; why 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … are called square numbers; and why 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, … are called cubes.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe that 36 is both a triangular number and a square number; draw pictures showing 36 dots arranged as both a triangle and a square, and explore other numbers that can be represented pictorially in multiple ways.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.3 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the sequence 1, 7, 19, 37, … as hexagonal numbers from a given dot diagram; draw these in a notebook and find the next number in the sequence.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.5
homework.description: Devise pictorial ways to visualise the sequences of powers of 2 and powers of 3 using dot or geometric diagrams.

time_bands.activity: Students open Table 2 and study the dot diagrams without writing. Ask: 'Why is the third triangular-number diagram shaped the way it is?' After a brief think-pair-share, students begin Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.5 ("Copy each pictorial representation from Table 2 and draw the next picture…."), copying and extending the diagrams for counting numbers, odd numbers, and even numbers in their notebooks.

Students continue Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.5 for the triangular, square, and cube dot diagrams, then move immediately to Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.5 ("Explain geometrically why 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … are called triangular numbers…."). They write a geometric explanation in their own words — the diagram itself is part of the answer. Invite two or three students to share their explanations aloud, emphasising the shape the dots form.

Students investigate Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.5 ("Observe that 36 is both a triangular number and a square number….") by drawing 36 dots both ways, then attempt Figure it Out Q4, section 1.3 p.5 ("Identify the sequence 1, 7, 19, 37, … as hexagonal numbers…."), drawing the hexagonal dot patterns and finding the next term. Close by asking: 'What tells you the next hexagonal number without counting every dot?' — eliciting the idea of a formation rule visible in the geometry.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the formation rules for the ten sequences in Table 1, students now build geometric intuition for why those rules work — the dot diagram is not decoration but explanation. A common error is drawing the 'square' diagram as a rectangle; prompt students to count rows and columns and confirm they are equal. Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.5 ("Devise pictorial ways to visualise the sequences of powers of 2 and powers of 3….") is set as a take-home creative task so students can experiment without time pressure.

periods.activity_title: Gnomon Proof: Why Odd Sums Make Squares

textbook_items_in_class.description: Shows that summing successive odd numbers (1, 1+3, 1+3+5, …) always yields square numbers, and provides a visual dot-grid proof by partitioning any n×n square into L-shaped gnomons of 1, 3, 5, … dots, explaining why the pattern holds for any square.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find a pictorial explanation for why adding counting numbers up and down (1, 1+2+1, 1+2+3+2+1, …) gives square numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the pictorial insight to determine the value of the symmetric sum 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 99 + 100 + 99 + … + 3 + 2 + 1.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.4 p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: Investigate what sequence is produced by adding consecutive pairs of triangular numbers (1+3, 3+6, 6+10, …) and explain the result with a picture.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.4 p.8
homework.description: Determine what sequence is obtained by successively adding up the all 1's sequence, and what sequence results from adding the all 1's sequence up and then down.

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example, section 1.4 p.6 ("Shows that summing successive odd numbers … always yields square numbers….") as a whole-class demonstration. Draw the 4×4 dot grid on the board and show the L-shaped gnomons partitioning it into 1, 3, 5, 7 dots. Ask students to copy the diagram and annotate each gnomon with its odd number before the explanation continues — making the visual proof theirs, not just the teacher's.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.8 ("Find a pictorial explanation for why adding counting numbers up and down … gives square numbers."). They work individually — drawing, annotating, then comparing with a neighbour. The target insight is that the 'up and down' sum 1+2+…+n+…+2+1 fills an n×n grid just as the gnomons do, but from the diagonal outward. After sharing two approaches, move to Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.8 ("Use the pictorial insight to determine the value of the symmetric sum 1+2+3+…+100+…+2+1") — students apply the pattern to a large case without computing term by term.

In pairs, students investigate Figure it Out Q5, section 1.4 p.8 ("Investigate what sequence is produced by adding consecutive pairs of triangular numbers…."). They compute 1+3, 3+6, 6+10, 10+15 and check whether the results appear in Table 1. The pairing task requires both the arithmetic and a picture showing why two consecutive triangular dot arrays combine into a square. Circulate and ask: 'Can you draw it?' to push from numerical observation to geometric reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The gnomon diagram from the worked example is the visual engine for this entire unit; students who skip drawing it and work only numerically are likely to lose the reasoning thread when tackling Figure it Out Q5. A frequent error is computing the symmetric sum by brute-force addition rather than recognising it as 100² = 10 000 — use Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.8 to press on this. Figure it Out Q3, section 1.4 p.8 ("Determine what sequence is obtained by successively adding up the all 1's sequence….") is set as take-home to consolidate the 'successive sums' idea without crowding the class time.

periods.activity_title: Deep Relations: Powers, Hexagons, and Cubes

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 1.4 p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore running sums of powers of 2 (1, 1+2, 1+2+4, …) and find what sequence results from adding 1 to each partial sum; explain why.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 1.4 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Multiply each triangular number by 6 and add 1 (e.g., 1×6+1=7, 3×6+1=19, …); identify the resulting sequence and explain it with a picture.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 1.4 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Add up hexagonal numbers successively (1, 1+7, 1+7+19, …); identify the resulting sequence and explain it using a picture of a cube.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 1.4 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Discover own patterns or relations among the sequences in Table 1 and attempt to explain them with pictures or reasoning.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.4 p.8
homework.description: Identify the sequence obtained by successively adding the counting numbers (1, 1+2, 1+2+3, …) and provide a pictorial explanation.

time_bands.activity: Students compute the running sums of powers of 2 for Figure it Out Q6, section 1.4 p.8 ("Explore running sums of powers of 2 (1, 1+2, 1+2+4, …) and find what sequence results from adding 1 to each partial sum…."). After listing the partial sums (1, 3, 7, 15, 31, …) and then adding 1 to each (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, …), students identify the resulting sequence from Table 1 and articulate why: each partial sum is one less than the next power of 2.

In pairs, students work on Figure it Out Q7, section 1.4 p.9 ("Multiply each triangular number by 6 and add 1…."). They compute the first four results, compare with Table 1, and identify hexagonal numbers. The follow-up is a sketch: can they draw a hexagonal dot pattern centred on 1 dot and see six triangular 'arms'? Then students move to Figure it Out Q8, section 1.4 p.9 ("Add up hexagonal numbers successively (1, 1+7, 1+7+19, …)…."), computing the running sums (1, 8, 27, …) and recognising cube numbers — the picture of a cube built from unit cubes is the requested explanation.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q9, section 1.4 p.9 ("Discover own patterns or relations among the sequences in Table 1….") individually, choosing any two sequences from Table 1 and testing a relationship. They write one conjecture — a sentence of the form 'I notice that…' — and attempt a numerical check or a sketch. A few students share their conjectures; the class decides whether each holds for the next term too, practising the habit of verification.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently verify a pattern for two or three cases and declare it proved; Figure it Out Q9, section 1.4 p.9 is the ideal moment to insist on at least four cases before trusting a conjecture. The connection between triangular numbers and hexagonal numbers in Figure it Out Q7 surprises most students — let them sit with the surprise before offering the picture. Figure it Out Q4, section 1.4 p.8 ("Identify the sequence obtained by successively adding the counting numbers….") is given as take-home because it consolidates the 'successive sums give triangular numbers' idea that students should discover without time pressure.

periods.activity_title: Shape Sequences and Their Hidden Number Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Recognise the formation pattern or rule in each of the five shape sequences presented in Table 3.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.5 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Redraw each of the five shape sequences from Table 3; attempt to draw the next shape in each sequence and describe the rule in own words.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.6 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Count the number of sides and corners in each regular polygon in the sequence; identify which number sequence is produced and explain why sides and corners always give the same count.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.6 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Count the number of lines in each complete graph (K2 through K6); identify the resulting number sequence and explain why it forms that pattern.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.6 p.12
homework.description: Count the total line segments in each Koch snowflake iteration and identify the corresponding number sequence (3, 12, 48, … = 3 × powers of 4).

time_bands.activity: Introduce Table 3 from section 1.5 and the idea that shapes, like numbers, can form sequences with rules. Students study Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.11 ("Recognise the formation pattern or rule in each of the five shape sequences….") silently, then name the rule for each of the five sequences to a partner. Draw attention to the Koch snowflake — invite students to describe in words what is happening to each line segment at every step before anyone attempts to draw it.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 1.5 p.11 ("Redraw each of the five shape sequences from Table 3; attempt to draw the next shape…."). They redraw and extend at least three sequences, writing a one-sentence rule for each. The Koch snowflake extension is attempted as a challenge; students who find it intricate are encouraged to describe the rule in words rather than force a perfect drawing. Collect two or three volunteers to put their next-Koch sketch on the board for class comparison.

Pivot to section 1.6 using the Example, section 1.6 p.11 ("Identifies that the regular polygon sequence encodes the counting numbers starting at 3….") as the worked illustration. Students then complete Figure it Out Q1, section 1.6 p.11 ("Count the number of sides and corners in each regular polygon….") and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.6 p.11 ("Count the number of lines in each complete graph K2 through K6…."), filling a small table of counts and identifying which sequences from Table 1 appear.

Rapid class discussion: students share the number sequences hidden in the stacked-squares and stacked-triangles shape sequences from Figure it Out Q3, section 1.6 p.12 ("Count the unit squares in each shape of the stacked squares sequence….") and Figure it Out Q4, section 1.6 p.12 ("Count the unit triangles in each shape of the stacked triangles sequence…."), identifying square numbers in both. Close by asking: 'Why do two very different shapes produce the same number sequence?' — leaving the question as an open invitation to further thought.

periods.teacher_notes: Geometry as a source of number sequences is the surprise payoff of section 1.6; students who have been working only with Table 1 often do not expect their number results to reappear here. Watch for students counting lines in complete graphs by re-drawing each edge rather than reasoning systematically — Figure it Out Q2, section 1.6 p.11 is a good prompt to ask 'Is there a faster way to count?' nudging the triangular-number reasoning. Figure it Out Q5, section 1.6 p.12 ("Count the total line segments in each Koch snowflake iteration….") is set as take-home because the Koch counting task rewards careful, unhurried work.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes what mathematics is primarily concerned with, according to section 1.1?

options.label: A
options.text: Performing calculations quickly using standard formulas.

options.label: B
options.text: Searching for patterns and explaining why those patterns exist.

options.label: C
options.text: Memorising number tables and geometric shapes.

options.label: D
options.text: Translating word problems into arithmetic operations.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Mathematics is, in large part, the search for patterns and the explanations for why those patterns exist; it is framed as both an art and a science.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the opening definition of mathematics from section 1.1 as pattern-finding and explanation.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student associates mathematics primarily with speed and computation, missing the pattern-and-explanation framing of section 1.1.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates mathematics with rote memorisation, the very approach section 1.1 moves away from.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student reduces mathematics to translation of word problems, overlooking the broader search for patterns and understanding.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the opening paragraph of section 1.1 and underline the sentence that defines what mathematics is.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write one more example — beyond those in the section — where a pattern in nature led to a scientific discovery.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.2
exercise.description: Think of other examples where mathematics helps in everyday life (shopping, cooking, speed, area, design, etc.).

items.prompt: Table 3 in section 1.5 presents five shape sequences. Which branch of mathematics is named in section 1.5 as the one that studies patterns in shapes?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — Section 1.5 names geometry as the branch of mathematics that studies patterns in shapes in one, two, three, or more dimensions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the direct statement in section 1.5 naming geometry as the study of patterns in shapes.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recalls section 1.2's naming of number theory but has not yet separated the two named branches from their respective domains.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student guesses a familiar term rather than recalling the specific term used in section 1.5.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates shape-patterns with data representation rather than the geometric study of shape sequences.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to locate the sentence in section 1.5 that names the branch and read it aloud.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to name one other phenomenon in real life — beyond the five in Table 3 — that could be described as a shape sequence.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.11
exercise.description: Recognise the formation pattern or rule in each of the five shape sequences presented in Table 3.

items.prompt: The fourth triangular number is 10. Draw a dot diagram showing 10 dots arranged as a triangle. Using your diagram, explain in one or two sentences why the sequence 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … deserves to be called 'triangular numbers.'

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A correct diagram shows 10 dots arranged in 4 rows containing 1, 2, 3, and 4 dots respectively, forming a triangular shape. The explanation should state that these numbers are called triangular because the dots can always be arranged into an equilateral triangle shape, with each new term adding one extra row at the base.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the dot-diagram visualisation from Table 2 to connect the geometric shape to the number sequence's name.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student look at Table 2 in section 1.3 and count the rows in the triangular dot picture before drawing their own.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why adding one extra row each time ensures the shape remains a triangle rather than some other polygon.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.5
exercise.description: Copy each pictorial representation from Table 2 and draw the next picture in each dot-diagram sequence.

items.prompt: The worked example in section 1.4 shows that 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16, which is 4². A student claims: 'The sum of the first 5 odd numbers must equal 5² = 25.' Without adding the numbers one by one, explain in one or two sentences why this claim is correct, using the idea of L-shaped gnomons.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The claim is correct. A 5×5 dot grid contains 25 dots. It can be partitioned into five L-shaped gnomons containing 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 dots respectively — each gnomon is an odd number, and together they fill the entire square — so the sum of the first 5 odd numbers equals the total dot count, which is 5² = 25.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the gnomon partition argument from the worked example: an n×n dot grid is partitioned into n L-shaped gnomons of 1, 3, 5, …, (2n−1) dots, so the sum equals n².

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to sketch a 5×5 dot grid and draw at least the first two L-shaped gnomons before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if you change the claim to 'the first 5 odd numbers starting from 3,' does a similar square still appear? What happens and why?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.8
exercise.description: Find a pictorial explanation for why adding counting numbers up and down (1, 1+2+1, 1+2+3+2+1, …) gives square numbers.

items.prompt: The running sums of the powers of 2 are: 1, 1+2=3, 1+2+4=7, 1+2+4+8=15, 1+2+4+8+16=31. Add 1 to each of these partial sums and write the resulting sequence. What sequence from Table 1 does this produce? Show your working and explain in one sentence why adding 1 always gives the next power of 2.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Adding 1 to each partial sum gives 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 — which is the powers of 2 sequence (starting from 2¹). The explanation: the sum of the first n powers of 2 (starting from 2⁰ = 1) equals 2ⁿ − 1, so adding 1 yields 2ⁿ, the next power of 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the pattern that the partial sum of powers of 2 up to 2^(n−1) equals 2ⁿ − 1, so adding 1 recovers 2ⁿ.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to write the running sums in a table with three columns: running sum, +1, result — and check whether the 'result' column matches any column in Table 1.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to test whether a similar rule holds for powers of 3: do the running sums of 1, 3, 9, 27, … also give a neat result when you add 2 to each?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 1.4 p.8
exercise.description: Explore running sums of powers of 2 (1, 1+2, 1+2+4, …) and find what sequence results from adding 1 to each partial sum; explain why.

items.prompt: A regular hexagon has 6 sides and 6 corners. A student says: 'For every regular polygon, the number of sides and the number of corners are always equal.' Using the explanation from section 1.6, justify in one or two sentences why this must be true for any closed polygon, not just regular ones.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In any closed polygon, each corner is the point where exactly two sides meet, and each side connects exactly two corners. This one-to-one correspondence means every side corresponds to exactly one corner and vice versa, so the count of sides must always equal the count of corners — for regular and irregular polygons alike.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the reasoning from section 1.6's worked example: in any closed polygon, sides and corners correspond one-to-one, making their counts equal.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to draw a quadrilateral, label each side with a letter and each corner with a number, and count whether the labels and numbers match up.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: does the same equal-count rule extend to three-dimensional shapes like a cube? What is different there, and why?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.6 p.11
exercise.description: Count the number of sides and corners in each regular polygon in the sequence; identify which number sequence is produced and explain why sides and corners always give the same count.
